Week 6 — Validate the use; how an app is built

A number can be correctly sourced (week 4) and correctly defended (week 5) and still be the wrong number for the question. This week you ask: fit for what purpose, for whom? First half: whose population does your measure cover, which hospitals are missing and why, and what happens when county data is attached to hospitals. You end with your data card. Second half: how a marimo notebook becomes an app, and an optional one-screen sketch of the app you'll build.

2. Coverage by hospital type and state

A layer that covers acute-care hospitals well may say nothing about critical-access, psychiatric or children's hospitals. Your data card must say which.By state (sort by clicking a column header): which states would your app describe poorly?

data.text/markdown:
3. County data attached to hospitals: the ecological fallacy

If your layer joins a county measure (CDC PLACES, ACS) to hospitals, every hospital in a county gets the same county value. In the course crosswalk, 88 hospitals sit in Los Angeles County, CA (FIPS 06037), and 897 counties have more than one hospital. A county value describes people who live in the county — it is a fact about a place, not about any hospital's patients. So "hospitals in high-poverty counties have higher readmissions" is a statement about counties. It does not show that poorer patients are readmitted more, and it can't tell you anything about one patient. Saying otherwise is the ecological fallacy. Patients also cross county lines. Coverage gap to put on your data card: 325 hospitals that have a county FIPS get no CDC PLACES 2025 value at all, because their county code is not in the PLACES file (by state: PA 186, KY 103, CT 36). Find out why before you explain it — don't guess.

5. How an app is built and published

A marimo app is just a notebook with controls (mo.ui.…) and outputs that depend on them. When a control changes, marimo re-runs every cell that uses it — nothing else. That's the whole idea. Below is a complete tiny app in two cells. The code is shown because reading it is the lesson:
  • Cell 1 makes a control. mo.ui.dropdown(...) builds the menu; the last line (state) displays it.
  • Cell 2 uses state.value — whatever the user picked. Because it mentions state, marimo re-runs it on every change. It filters to that state, counts hospitals by type, and draws a bar chart with altair. The title says how many rows are behind the chart — always show that.
